title: Present Value
subtitle: How much is a dong received in the future worth today?
openingQuestion: If the interest rate is 10%/year, what is the present value of 1 million received after 1 year?
explanation: Present value converts a future amount back to today by dividing by one plus the interest rate, raised to the number of years. The idea underneath is simple: money today can be invested to earn a return, so it's worth more than the same amount received later. Two consequences to remember - the higher the discount rate, the lower the present value, and the further out a cash flow is, the faster it shrinks because of the exponent. All of financial valuation is built on this calculation.

diagram.label: An amount to be received in the future
Choose a discount rate matching that amount's risk
Divide by (1+r) raised to the number of years
Get the present value - now comparable against money today

realWorldExample.description: The price of any bond on the market is essentially the sum of the Present Value of the coupon payments and face value to be received in the future, discounted back to today at the market yield - this is the most direct and common real-world application of Present Value.

quiz.question: Why does a higher discount rate reduce Present Value?
options: Because risk falls, making future cash flow more trustworthy than the present
Because opportunity cost is higher - money today can earn more
Because rising inflation reduces the nominal value of the cash flow
Because the formula just says so, with no underlying economic reason
quiz.explanation: A higher discount rate = higher opportunity cost = future money is worth less relative to today. When interest rates rise, the PV of every future cash flow falls → stock and bond prices fall.

quiz.question: If the discount rate falls from 10% to 5%, how will the Present Value of an amount received in the future change?
options: It falls, because a lower interest rate makes future money earn less
It doesn't change since FV and the number of years are unchanged
It rises - a smaller r means a smaller denominator, so a larger PV
It only changes if the number of discounting years also changes
quiz.explanation: PV = FV / (1+r)^n - the smaller r is, the smaller the denominator, the larger PV becomes. This is exactly why, when market interest rates fall, the valuation of stocks and bonds rises.

quiz.question: Receiving 1,000,000 dong after 5 years, discount rate 10%. What is the PV?
options: ≈ 1,610,500 dong (= 1M × 1.61, multiplying instead of dividing)
≈ 500,000 dong (= 1M ÷ 2, halved for 5 years)
≈ 909,100 dong (= 1M ÷ 1.1, discounting only 1 year)
≈ 620,900 dong (= 1M ÷ 1.1 to the 5th power, i.e. divided by 1.61)
quiz.explanation: PV = FV / (1+r)^n = 1,000,000 / 1.61051 ≈ 620,900 dong. The figure 1,610,500 dong is actually Future Value - multiplying moves you toward the future, dividing is what pulls you back to the present.

quiz.question: Two cash flows of 1 billion, one received after 3 years, one after 10 years, at the same discount rate. Compare their PV.
options: The 3-year cash flow has higher PV since it's discounted fewer times
The two cash flows have equal PV since the nominal amount is identical
The 10-year cash flow is higher because it has more time to compound
They can't be compared without knowing if the cash flow grows
quiz.explanation: The denominator (1+r)^n grows exponentially as n increases. This is why in a DCF model, cash flows from the final years contribute far less even though the nominal figures might be larger.

quiz.question: Why is PV the foundation of every valuation model?
options: Because it removes the impact of inflation from cash flow
Because it converts cash flows at different points in time onto the same footing
Because it tells you whether a business has enough cash to pay its debts
Because it's the only metric that doesn't depend on any assumption
quiz.explanation: You can't add 100 million from this year to 100 million from year seven - they're two different units. Discounting is the conversion that lets you add them together, and every DCF model is just a chain of that same conversion repeated.

keyTakeaways: The foundation of DCF valuation and every investment decision

practicePrompt.question: You are promised 121 million dong to be received in 2 years. If a reasonable discount rate is 10%/year, what is the present value (PV) of this amount?
options: PV = FV / (1+r)^n = 121 / (1.1)² = 100 million dong, which is what that sum is worth today
PV = FV × (1+r)^n = 121 × 1.21 = 146.4 million dong, since you must multiply by interest for each waiting year
PV always exactly equals FV = 121 million because money's value doesn't change over time
PV cannot be calculated without knowing exactly who the company or individual promising to pay is
practicePrompt.explanation: PV = FV / (1+r)^n = 121,000,000 / (1.1)^2 = 100,000,000 dong. This is the discounting formula: present value is always smaller than future value because a dong today can earn a return over time (time value of money).

summary.commonMistake: Reading a concept as a phrase to memorise rather than a principle to apply to real decisions.

application.title: Calculate PV yourself
application.message: Pick an amount you might receive in the future (a bonus, salary, money lent), assume a reasonable discount rate, and calculate for yourself how much it's worth today.
application.secondary: Choose a higher discount rate when you feel the risk of receiving that amount is greater.

sections.text: A dong received in the future is worth less than a dong in hand today, because today's dong can be invested to earn a return immediately. Present Value (PV) answers the reverse question: an amount X received after n years - how much is that worth today? This question sits at the root of every financial valuation - from stock prices, to bond prices, to whether a project is worth investing in.

PV = FV / (1+r)^n, where FV is the future amount, r is the discount rate (reflecting opportunity cost), and n is the number of years. **Example:** receiving 1,000,000 dong after 1 year, discount rate 10%. PV = 1,000,000 / 1.1 = 909,091 dong. That means if you had 909,091 dong today and deposited it at 10% interest, after 1 year you'd have exactly 1,000,000 dong - the two amounts are 'worth the same.'
PV falls as n rises or r rises

The same 1,000,000 dong received after 5 years instead of 1 year: PV = 1,000,000 / (1.1)^5 = 1,000,000 / 1.61051 ≈ 620,921 dong - much lower. The further into the future, the smaller the PV. Similarly, if the discount rate rises from 10% to 15%, the PV of the same amount 1 year later falls to 1,000,000 / 1.15 ≈ 869,565 dong. A higher discount rate means the 'cost' of waiting is higher.

items: PV is the foundation for bond valuation: bond price = PV of coupons + PV of face value
PV is the foundation for equity valuation via DCF: business value = PV of future free cash flow
The higher the discount rate (the greater the risk), the lower the PV, even if future cash flow doesn't change
Don't confuse PV with 'the amount to be received' - PV is always smaller than the nominal future amount when r > 0

sections.label: Why rising interest rates push stock prices down
sections.text: When market interest rates rise, the discount rate used to value every asset rises with it → the PV of future cash flow falls → stock and bond valuations fall, even though the business itself hasn't changed at all.

lines: PV is the question 'how much is future money worth today' - the foundational question of every valuation.
Remember the formula PV = FV/(1+r)^n, and the rest of the Time Value of Money track is just variations on it.
